value: six eyes: AME largest and dark; ALE and PLE pale, translucent
method: taxonomic description of preserved type specimens
conditions: Description of the male holotype (IAvH-I 3747; Boyacá Department, Santuario de Flora y Fauna Iguaque, El Caimo, Sector Chaina, 2730 m, 24 Sep. 2003). Five paratypes: 2 males and 3 females (same locality; Villa de Leyva, Colegio Antonio Nariño, 2200 m; Vereda Sopotá, Finca El Peladero, 2185 m). The female description says only 'Carapace and eyes as in male.' The Discussion states 'Representatives of Caponina have between 4 and 6 eyes (with aberrant individuals with 3 or 5 eyes, respectively, as reported by Platnick 1994a)' and that Caponina are the only caponiids with a variable number of eyes among species; the emended diagnosis contrasts Calponia and Caponia (eight eyes), genera with two eyes and Carajas (no eyes). The Diagnoses of the three new species carry no eye wording and no species account has a Remarks section. The identification key separates 'Six eyes (rarely five)' from 'Four eyes (rarely three)'.

value: first-instar larva without compound eyes, ocelli or stemmata
method: light and scanning electron microscopy of first-instar larvae
conditions: First-instar larvae only (white, 2.9 ± 0.31 mm long, n = 10), obtained from adults collected at Huaboshan (41°06'N, 125°02'E, 650-1100 m), Kuandian County, Liaoning Province, China, in late June to July 2011 and 2012 and reared in pairs; the article does not state how many larvae were examined for SEM and does not say the larvae hatched in the laboratory. The General morphology section also says 'The head is hypognathous and eyeless'. The Abstract and Discussion call the larva of Panorpodes eyeless ('completely eyeless, congruent with the larvae of Brachypanorpa') and contrast it with Mecoptera in general, whose larvae have 'a pair of compound eyes' (Bittacidae with a dorsal ocellus and seven ommatidia, Panorpidae about 20-40 ommatidia, Boreus three stemmata). Later instars are not described.

conditions: Description of the last-instar larva ('Larva, last instar. Length 5.0-7.0 mm'). The sentence does not say whether six is the count per side or in all; the paper also describes the pupa's eyes separately. The paper compares larvae of co-occurring dermestid genera in a table (Table 2); its '# of stemmata' column (Table 2.3) gives 6 for Ctesias, as for Dermestes (footnote: D. depressus lacks stemmata), Trinodes, Anthrenus and Globicornis, against 3 in Thylodrias, 4-5 in Attagenus, 4 in Reesa and 5 in Trogoderma, and does not say per side or in all either.

method: estimate from facet density on exceptionally preserved Middle Jurassic specimens (Supplementary Note 1)
conditions: Fossil thylacocephalan arthropod, early Callovian, La Voulte-sur-Rhône Lagerstätte, Ardèche, France; three-dimensionally preserved specimens; the text gives no count, and the figure legends name eight Dollocaris ingens specimens (MNHN.F.R50939, MHNL-20293244, MNHN.F.R06202, UJF-ID-1799, FSL 710067, FSL 710064, MNHN.F.A29278, MNHN.F.R06206), Fig. 2a being FSL 710064; the facet-counted specimens are not named in the text read. The count is derived: the preceding sentence gives an estimated surface density of more than 500 ommatidia per mm2, and the Discussion gives the number as estimated 'to ∼18,000 on the basis of facet countings in well-preserved specimens and assuming that each eye is approximately an hemisphere with evenly distributed ommatidia' (a calculated total, not a count), and calls it 'a rough estimate that does not take into account possible local variations of the bending radius and the ommatidial size'. The Abstract says 'about 18,000 lenses on each eye'. The value is per eye. Facets are about 40 µm across (a separate Results sentence).

value: roughly spherical main globe plus an extensive rostrolateral diverticulum with a sclerally derived lens
conditions: One eye of one specimen (standard length 200 mm; caught at 400-600 m in the North Atlantic on RRS Discovery 243 with a rectangular midwater trawl, one of four species caught specifically for the study); Table 1 gives eye height 7.5 mm, width 9.2 mm, lens diameter 4.5 mm. Histology, Figures 5 and 6. Other species in the paper (Opisthoproctus soleatus, Winteria telescopa, Rhynchohyalus natalensis, Dolichopteryx longipes, Macropinna microstoma) are not covered by this record. The Introduction groups the bipartite eyes of D. longipes, R. natalensis and B. exilis; the Figure 10 legend calls the rostrolateral diverticulum 'characterised by a prominent, sclerally derived, lens' and shows light focused on the diverticular retina only 'on the unproven assumption that the scleral lens is sufficiently refractive'; the Abstract says the diverticula form images 'using either reflection or possibly refraction'.

method: microscope measurement of a preserved larva
conditions: Wild-caught larvae and juveniles from the Sheyang Sea Area (Jiangsu Province, Yellow Sea), April 2017, identified by COI barcoding; stage counts printed are 6 yolk-sac larvae, 67 preflexion larvae and 182 juveniles, none for flexion. No measurement table: eye diameters sit in the running text as single values per stage with no n, mean or range, and the preflexion text gives two values (0.22 and 0.24 mm). The Discussion has no comparison of eye development with other Pholis species. This value is for the flexion larva (total length 10.65 mm, body length 10.31 mm, head length 1.28 mm), one specimen, which the Figure 3 and 4 legends label '10.31 mm BL flexion larva'. Measured under a Nikon SMZ 25 stereomicroscope; the Methods list eye diameter among the measurements but do not define it.
